newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. and China fail to end human rights impasse.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and China fail to end human rights impasse.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore met senior Chinese officials on Tuesday to begin the highest level U.S. diplomatic talks in Beijing in eight years but the bid to defuse differences failed to end an impasse over human rights.
Gore assured his hosts that allegations China tried to illegally influence U.S. elections last year would not deflect Washington from a policy of engagement with Beijing.
He also presided over signings of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China -- signalling that once chilly ties between Beijing and Washington were thawing.
A U.S. official who attended Gore's meetings with Chinese Premier Li Peng said Li vigorously denied the allegations of illegal payments to the U.S. Democratic Party.
Gore told Li the issue was being investigated "but the important point was that this in no way would deflect the administration from pursuing its policy of engagement with China", the official said.
Li responded by saying he was assured this would not affect Washington's pledges to improve ties with Beijing, the official added.
Discussion on the issue, which has cast a shadow over Gore's visit, lasted for several minutes.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
Gore launched his first full day in China with a series of high-level talks and is scheduled to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday.
Members of the U.S. delegation said little had been achieved to bridge the gap between the two countries on human rights but talks on the issue were less acrimonious than in the past.
"We had a very productive and energetic talk," Gore told a news briefing in the Great Hall of the People.
"The meetings today were very positive. Both sides have a desire to lend forward momentum...recognising areas where we agreed to disagree."

Gore is the most senior U.S. official to visit China since Beijing crushed student-led protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989. His trip is designed to pave the way for an exchange of visits over the next year.
Political activists said Beijing police had told the tiny band of dissidents in the city not to leave their homes during Gore's visit and had stepped up surveillance of their families.
China appeared keen that disputes over human rights should not be allowed to overshadow business gains.
"There are in fact differences between China and the United States on some issues, including differences on human rights," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
"It would not be possible for there to be no differences between two such big nations with such contrasting cultures."
In a sign of rapidly improving ties between the United States and its fastest-growing Pacific neighbour, Gore and Li witnessed the signings of two major business deals.

Boeing Co signed a deal to sell five 777-200 aircraft worth $685 million to China's international carrier, Air China. General Motors Corp launched a long-delayed joint venture with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp to build medium-sized cars.

Analysts said the Chinese decision to buy the new generation aircraft was almost certainly based not only on aviation needs but on a thaw in relations. Sino-U.S. relations chilled in 1995 and early 1996 amid disputes over human rights and Taiwan.
Despite the good cheer the contracts generated, Li sounded a note of caution which reflected China's concern about growing U.S. influence in world affairs.
"We believe the United States, the biggest developed country in the world, should play a more positive role in international affairs," Li said.

U.S. officials dismissed reports that Gore hesitated about attending the signing ceremonies because of the allegations that China had tried to influence last year's U.S. elections by illegally funnelling cash to support President Bill Clinton's campaign.
"These agreements...are proof positive that there is greater economic cooperation between the United States and China," said Ginny Terzano, Gore's press secretary.
Under a third agreement signed on Tuesday, China will formally allow Washington to maintain a consulate in Hong Kong after British colonial rule ends at midnight on June 30.
